title: Sanhedrin 37a and Makkot 7a: One Life, and a Court That Rarely Kills
bigQuestion: How can a legal system that allows the death penalty also work hard to keep it from being used?

story.title: If We Had Sat on the Court
story.kicker: Two famous rabbis say that under them, no one would ever have been executed.
paragraphs: The Mishnah in tractate Makkot, chapter 1, is discussing courts. It gives a surprising line. A Sanhedrin that puts a person to death once in seven years is called destructive. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah goes further: once in seventy years. The Mishnah is describing a court that almost never kills.

Then two great sages speak. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say that if they had been on the Sanhedrin, no person would ever have been executed. The Gemara on Makkot 7a asks how. It answers with the kind of questions they would ask witnesses, questions so exact that testimony would almost always fail.

But the Mishnah gives one more voice. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel answers: they too would multiply murderers in Israel. A court that never punishes, he warns, may fail to protect people. The Mishnah does not settle the debate. It ends with both views standing.

This chapter reads two passages. One is Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, with its famous line that one life is a whole world. The other is Makkot 7a. Together they show a body of law that keeps capital punishment on the books, surrounds it with protections, and argues about whether to use it at all.
story.think: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel worries about the victims of crime. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon worry about the accused. How could both concerns come from mercy?

lessons.title: Warning the Witnesses
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 describes how judges warned witnesses in capital cases about the weight of a human life.
reading: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 begins in a courtroom. In a capital case, the judges bring in the witnesses and warn them. Perhaps you are speaking from guesswork, or from rumor, or from what another witness said. Perhaps you did not know we would question you closely.

Then the Mishnah explains why capital cases are different. In money cases, a false witness can pay money back. In capital cases, the blood of the accused and of his descendants that might have been is on the witness until the end of the world. The warning is meant to make a witness afraid of lying or guessing.

The Mishnah then reads Genesis 4:10, where God tells Cain, the voice of your brother's blood cries. In Hebrew the word for blood is plural, bloods. The Mishnah takes this as meaning Abel's blood and the blood of all his descendants who would never be born. One death cuts off a future.

words.d: a rabbinic court; the tractate describes courts of 23 and of 71 judges
a case in which the penalty could be death
a person who testifies to what they saw; the Torah requires two in capital cases

look.title: The warning to witnesses
look.text: Know that capital cases are not like money cases. In money cases, a person can pay and be forgiven. In capital cases, the blood of the accused and of his offspring hang on the witness to the end of the world.
look.cite: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, paraphrased from the Hebrew (compare Danby, The Mishnah, 1933; Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 37a)
look.prompt: Why would the court want witnesses to feel this weight before they speak?

check.q: In Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, who is warned before a capital case?
check.why: The judges warn the witnesses.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say capital cases differ from money cases?
choices: Money can be repaid, but a life and its descendants cannot
Money cases are decided by a heavenly voice
check.why: The Mishnah contrasts repayable money with an irreversible life.

check.q: What detail in Genesis 4:10 does the Mishnah read closely?
choices: The word for blood is plural
check.why: 'Bloods' is read to include Abel's unborn descendants.

lessons.title: Why One Person Was Created
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah teaches that humanity began with a single person, so that destroying one life is like destroying a world.
reading: The Mishnah continues: for this reason a single human being was created. It points to Adam, the first person in Genesis. Because all of humanity came from one person, each person carries a whole world within them. The Mishnah draws a legal and moral rule from the creation story.

Its most famous line follows. Whoever destroys a single soul, Scripture counts it as if they destroyed a full world. Whoever saves a single soul, Scripture counts it as if they saved a full world. This line is quoted on buildings, awards and memorials, and in films and speeches around the world.

The Mishnah lists other reasons too. People cannot say, my ancestor was greater than yours, since all share one ancestor. And the Mishnah uses a picture: a human king stamps coins with one seal and they all look alike. The Holy One, it says, stamped every person with the seal of the first human, yet no two are alike.

words.d: the first human in Genesis; the Mishnah uses him to teach the worth of each person
a stamp that makes the same mark each time, like a coin die
the Genesis 1:27 idea that humans are made in God's image, which the Mishnah echoes

look.title: The coin and the person
look.text: A mint stamps a thousand coins with one die, and every coin is the same. The Mishnah says each human is stamped with the first human's seal, yet each one is different.
look.prompt: What point about human worth does this picture make? Why use money as the example?

check.q: Why was one person created first, according to Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5?
choices: Because there was not enough land
So the Sanhedrin could have 71 judges
To teach that one life is like a whole world
check.why: The Mishnah draws the worth of each life from creation.

check.q: In the Mishnah's picture, how is God's seal different from a king's?
choices: Every person has the same seal, yet no two are alike
It makes gold instead of silver
It is used only on kings
It is kept in the Temple
check.why: A king's coins match; people, the Mishnah says, are each unique.

check.q: Which social lesson does the Mishnah draw from one ancestor?
choices: Only one person may be a judge
No one can say their ancestor was greater
Each person must build a city
check.why: A shared ancestor means shared dignity.

lessons.title: Two Versions of the Line
lessons.mainIdea: Manuscripts and printed editions differ on whether the line says one soul or one soul of Israel.
reading: The famous line exists in two versions. Many printed editions of the Babylonian Talmud read: whoever destroys a single soul of Israel. Some important manuscripts of the Mishnah and the Jerusalem Talmud read simply: a single soul. Scholars have compared these texts for more than a century.

Many scholars think the shorter, universal wording is earlier, since the Mishnah's argument is about Adam, the ancestor of all people. Others note that the longer wording appears in many traditional editions and has been read and taught for centuries. Both versions are part of the history of the text.

The line also has a parallel outside Judaism. The Qur'an, in Surah 5:32, speaks of the Children of Israel being told that killing one person is like killing all people, and saving one is like saving all. Muslim and Jewish readers have discussed this connection. This lesson simply notes the parallel and its source.

words.d: a handwritten copy of a text, made before printing
a difference in wording between copies of a text
a text produced by printing press, such as the Vilna Talmud of the 1880s

look.title: How the text reached readers
look.cite: Common scholarly dates; Bomberg edition, Venice, 1520–1523; Romm edition, Vilna, 1880s
look.prompt: Between which two steps would scribes' handwritten copies have been the only way the text traveled?

check.q: What is the difference between the two versions of the line?
choices: One mentions Cain, the other does not
One is in Greek, the other in Hebrew
One says 'a single soul,' the other 'a single soul of Israel'
One is from Makkot, the other from Berakhot
check.why: The variant concerns the words 'of Israel'.

check.q: Why do many scholars think the universal wording is earlier?
choices: It is found only in modern books
It was voted on by the Sanhedrin
The Mishnah's argument is about Adam, ancestor of all people
check.why: The logic of the passage concerns all humanity.

check.q: Where is a parallel to the line found in the Qur'an?
check.why: Surah 5:32 contains a similar teaching.

sections.title: How the Court Protected the Accused

lessons.title: Twenty-Three Judges
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah requires a court of twenty-three for capital cases and builds rules that tilt toward acquittal.
reading: Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:4 says capital cases are judged by a court of twenty-three. Money cases need only three. The Great Sanhedrin, with seventy-one, handled the gravest national questions. The larger court for life-and-death cases meant more minds and more chances to find doubt.

Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1 lists the differences. In capital cases, the court opens with arguments for acquittal. A majority of one is enough to acquit, but conviction needs a majority of two. A judge who argued to acquit may not switch to convict, though a judge who argued to convict may switch to acquit.

Other rules follow. A verdict of acquittal can be given the same day, but conviction must wait until the next day. In capital cases the youngest judges speak first, so they are not swayed by their elders, according to Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:2. Each rule makes an execution harder to reach.

words.d: a verdict that the accused is not guilty
a verdict that the accused is guilty
in the Mishnah, the high court of seventy-one judges

look.title: Court sizes in the Mishnah
look.prompt: Why might a legal system want far more judges for a capital case than for a money case?

check.q: How many judges hear a capital case in the Mishnah?
check.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:4 requires twenty-three.

check.q: How large a majority does conviction require in a capital case?
check.why: Acquittal needs one; conviction needs two (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1).

check.q: Why do the youngest judges speak first in capital cases?
choices: So they are not swayed by their elders
check.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:2 gives this reason in effect.

lessons.title: Questioning the Witnesses
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah requires close questioning of witnesses, and any contradiction on key points ends the testimony.
reading: Mishnah Sanhedrin 5:1 says witnesses were examined with seven questions. In which seven-year cycle did it happen? In which year, month, day of the month, day of the week, hour and place? If the two witnesses disagreed on these, their testimony was thrown out.

The Mishnah also describes other checks. Did the witnesses recognize the accused? Did they warn him first? The rabbis read the Torah's rules, such as the need for two witnesses in Deuteronomy 17:6, very strictly. Each rule narrowed the path to a conviction.

The Mishnah even says the more a judge examines, the more praiseworthy he is. It tells how Ben Zakkai once questioned witnesses about the stems of figs under the tree. Details like these could reveal a false or mistaken witness. Such careful questioning protected the accused.

words.d: the court's close questioning of witnesses to test their testimony
the rabbinic rule that a person had to be warned before a crime could bring a court penalty
what a witness says under oath in court

look.title: Two witnesses
look.text: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he that is to die be put to death; at the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 17:6, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society, 1917
look.prompt: How does this verse already limit the death penalty before the rabbis add their own rules?

check.q: According to Mishnah Sanhedrin 5:1, how many basic questions were witnesses asked?
check.why: The Mishnah lists seven questions of time and place.

check.q: What happened if two witnesses contradicted each other on a key point?
choices: The case was sent to Elijah
check.why: Contradiction on the main questions voided the testimony.

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 17:6 require for a death sentence?
check.why: The verse forbids execution on one witness.

lessons.title: If All Convict, Acquit
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara records the striking view that if every judge votes to convict, the accused goes free.
reading: On Sanhedrin 17a, the Gemara reports a teaching from Rav Kahana, a Babylonian amora. If the Sanhedrin votes unanimously to convict, the accused is acquitted. At first this sounds backward. Surely a unanimous court is the most certain? Many students react that way on a first reading.

The Gemara's explanation is brief. The common explanation in later commentary is that a court with no one arguing for the accused has lost a needed voice. Without debate, the judges may be in a rush to judgment. Rashi and others explain that a court needs someone who searches for merit.

Legal historians find this rule remarkable. It treats disagreement as a safeguard. It fits the whole Talmud, which keeps minority opinions alive. Readers debate how practical it was, since the Talmud itself says capital cases had largely ceased by its editing.

words.d: a rabbi of the Gemara era, c. 200–500 CE
with every judge voting the same way
merit; an argument in favor of the accused

look.title: A unanimous vote
look.text: Imagine twenty-three judges. Every one of them votes guilty. Not a single judge found a reason to doubt. Rav Kahana says: acquit.
look.prompt: Is a unanimous verdict more trustworthy or less? Give a reason for each side before choosing.

check.q: On Sanhedrin 17a, what happens if all judges vote to convict?
choices: The accused is executed at once
check.why: Rav Kahana's teaching reverses the expected result.

check.q: What is an amora?
choices: A rabbi of the Gemara era, c. 200–500 CE
A rabbi of the Mishnah era
check.why: Amoraim follow the tannaim of the Mishnah.

check.q: What common explanation is given for Rav Kahana's rule?
choices: A court with no one arguing for the accused has lost a needed safeguard
Judges must disagree by law of Sinai
check.why: Commentators explain that no one searched for merit.

lessons.title: Once in Seven Years
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Makkot 1:10 calls a court that executes once in seven years destructive, and some say once in seventy.
reading: Mishnah Makkot 1:10 describes a Sanhedrin that executes once in seven years. It is called destructive. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says once in seventy years. The Gemara on Makkot 7a asks whether this means once in seven, or even less often. Either way, a court that kills often is condemned.

Then Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say that if they had been on the Sanhedrin, no one would ever have been executed. The Gemara asks how. Its answer is that they would have asked questions like: did you see whether the victim was already mortally wounded? Such questions could make a conviction almost impossible.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel responds that they would increase murderers in Israel. The Mishnah records his worry and does not answer it. The passage gives three positions: rare executions, no executions, and a warning that justice must still protect the public.

words.d: the Talmud tractate on lashes, false witnesses and cities of refuge; the name means 'Lashes'
a rabbi of the Mishnah era, before c. 200 CE
a second-century leader who warns against a court that never punishes

look.title: The destructive court
look.text: A Sanhedrin that executes once in seven years is called destructive. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says: once in seventy years. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: had we been on the Sanhedrin, no one would ever have been executed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: they would multiply murderers in Israel.
look.cite: Mishnah Makkot 1:10, discussed at Babylonian Talmud Makkot 7a, paraphrased (compare Danby, The Mishnah, 1933)
look.prompt: Which of the four speakers do you think gives the strongest argument? What does each protect?

check.q: What does Mishnah Makkot 1:10 call a court that executes once in seven years?
check.why: The Mishnah uses the word destructive.

check.q: Who says that under them no one would ever be executed?
check.why: Tarfon and Akiva speak together in the Mishnah.

check.q: What is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's worry?
choices: That a court that never executes would increase murderers
That the court has too many judges
That witnesses ask too many questions
check.why: He warns about public safety.

lessons.title: The Law Against Its Own Use
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars describe rabbinic capital law as a system written so strictly that it almost never allowed an execution.
reading: Put the pieces together. The Torah names crimes that carry the death penalty. The Mishnah keeps those laws. But it surrounds them with rules: two witnesses, warning beforehand, close questioning, a large court, a tilt to acquittal. The result, many scholars say, is a law that works against its own use.

History matters here. The Talmud reports that the Sanhedrin stopped hearing capital cases about forty years before the Temple fell in 70 CE (Sanhedrin 41a). Under Roman rule, Jewish courts likely lacked that power. So much of this law was studied, not practiced, by the rabbis who shaped it.

Readers disagree about what that means. Some see the rules as ideals from a time without such power. Others see them as a real legal philosophy. Many Jewish groups have drawn on these passages in modern debates about the death penalty. Their positions differ, and the course simply records the texts they cite.

words.d: punishment by execution, also called capital punishment
the period when Rome governed Judea, beginning in 63 BCE
law studied as a model of justice even when not practiced

look.title: Key dates for the courts
look.cite: Common historical dates; Sanhedrin 41a reports the end of capital jurisdiction c. 30 CE
look.prompt: By the time the Mishnah was edited, about how long had Jewish courts been without capital power, according to the Talmud's report?

check.q: According to Sanhedrin 41a, when did the Sanhedrin stop hearing capital cases?
choices: The day the Mishnah was written
About forty years before the Temple fell
check.why: The Talmud reports forty years before 70 CE.

check.q: What do many scholars mean by capital law working against its own use?
choices: The law was never written down
The rules made execution nearly impossible to reach
The Torah has no death penalty
check.why: The safeguards narrowed the path to conviction.

check.q: How does this course handle modern death-penalty debates?
choices: It argues for the death penalty
It argues against the death penalty
It records the texts groups cite without taking a side
check.why: The course describes, not decides.

lessons.title: Mercy and Justice in Tension
lessons.mainIdea: The sugyot keep two kinds of mercy in view: mercy for the accused and protection for possible victims.
reading: Both chapters of this unit end the same way. The Talmud does not give one simple answer. In Makkot, Akiva and Tarfon protect the accused, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel protects the public. In Bava Metzia, the majority decides the law, and the story defends the one who lost.

Each side has its own idea of mercy. Mercy for the accused asks that no innocent life be taken. Mercy for victims asks that the community be kept safe. Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 supports both, since it teaches that every life, the victim's and the accused's, is a whole world.

Many teachers today use these passages to train students in argument. They ask learners to state the strongest version of each side before choosing. That is the method of the chavruta, the study partnership. It fits a text that keeps both voices on the page.

words.d: a pair of study partners who read and argue about a text together
care that seeks to spare people from harm
giving each person what is right and fair under the law

look.title: Steelman both sides
look.text: Partner A defends Rabbi Akiva: better to free the guilty than kill the innocent. Partner B defends Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a court that never acts leaves victims unprotected.
look.prompt: With a partner, state the other side's best argument before your own. Which parts of Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 does each side use?

check.q: What is a chavruta?
check.why: Chavruta is the traditional study partnership.

check.q: How can Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 support both sides of the Makkot debate?
choices: It says only the accused matters
It teaches every life is a world, the victim's and the accused's
It says the majority is always right
check.why: The line applies to every life.

check.q: What do both of this unit's chapters show about the Talmud's method?
choices: It always sides with the majority
It keeps more than one view on the page instead of one simple answer
check.why: Both sugyot hold competing views together.

review.q: Which passage contains the line that saving one life is like saving a world?
review.why: The line is in Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5.

review.q: What does the Mishnah learn from the plural 'bloods' in Genesis 4:10?
choices: Abel's blood and that of his unborn descendants
review.why: The Mishnah reads the plural as including descendants.

review.q: How many judges hear capital cases in the Mishnah?
What does Rav Kahana teach on Sanhedrin 17a?
choices: If all judges convict, the accused is acquitted
review.why: A unanimous conviction leads to acquittal.

review.q: Who says a court that executes once in seventy years is destructive?
Who warns that Akiva and Tarfon would multiply murderers?
What is the difference between the two versions of the 'one soul' line?
review.why: Printed editions and some manuscripts differ on 'of Israel'.

review.q: Why was much rabbinic capital law studied rather than practiced?
choices: The rabbis did not know the law
Jewish courts under Rome likely lacked capital power
review.why: The Talmud reports capital cases ceased before 70 CE.
